title: GROUP BY and HAVING
description: Group your data into buckets with GROUP BY and filter those groups with HAVING — the counterpart to WHERE that runs after aggregation.

data.text: WHERE filters individual rows. HAVING filters entire groups. To get summary statistics per category, per store, or per month, you need GROUP BY paired with HAVING.
GROUP BY arranges rows into groups based on the values in one or more columns. After grouping, each aggregate function computes one value per group.

data.title: Basic GROUP BY with COUNT
data.code:
SELECT city, COUNT(customer_id) AS customer_count
FROM   sales.customers
GROUP BY city
ORDER BY customer_count DESC;

data.title: GROUP BY multiple columns
data.code:
SELECT state, city, COUNT(customer_id) AS customer_count
FROM   sales.customers
GROUP BY state, city
ORDER BY state, city;

items: Every column in the SELECT list must either appear in the GROUP BY clause or be wrapped in an aggregate function
GROUP BY treats NULL as a distinct value — all NULLs form one group together
The order of columns in GROUP BY affects which groupings you get (especially with ROLLUP/CUBE)

data.title: The #2 GROUP BY error
data.text: The most common GROUP BY mistake: including a column in SELECT that is not in GROUP BY and not aggregated. SQL Server will reject it with 'is invalid in the select list because it is not contained in either an aggregate function or the GROUP BY clause.'
HAVING applies conditions to groups after they are formed by GROUP BY. It is the group-level equivalent of WHERE — but while WHERE filters rows, HAVING filters the aggregated groups.

data.title: HAVING with COUNT
data.code:
SELECT city, COUNT(customer_id) AS customer_count
FROM   sales.customers
GROUP BY city
HAVING   COUNT(customer_id) >= 5
ORDER BY customer_count DESC;

data.title: HAVING with SUM
data.code:
SELECT order_id,
       SUM(quantity * list_price * (1 - discount)) AS net_value
FROM   sales.order_items
GROUP BY order_id
HAVING   SUM(quantity * list_price * (1 - discount)) > 20000
ORDER BY net_value;

data.title: HAVING with MIN and MAX
data.code:
SELECT category_id,
       MAX(list_price) AS max_price,
       MIN(list_price) AS min_price
FROM   production.products
GROUP BY category_id
HAVING   MAX(list_price) > 4000 OR MIN(list_price) < 500;

data.title: No aliases in HAVING
data.text: You cannot reference a column alias (like 'net_value') inside HAVING. You must repeat the full aggregate expression: HAVING SUM(...) > 20000, not HAVING net_value > 20000.

data.title: WHERE filters rows, then GROUP BY, then HAVING filters groups
data.code:
-- Find customers in California who placed 2+ orders
SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.first_name,
       c.last_name,
       COUNT(o.order_id) AS order_count
FROM   sales.customers c
INNER JOIN sales.orders o
    ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE  c.state = 'CA'
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.first_name, c.last_name
HAVING   COUNT(o.order_id) >= 2
ORDER BY order_count DESC;

data.text: This query illustrates the full pipeline: WHERE picks only California customers, GROUP BY assembles them into per-customer groups, the COUNT aggregate counts orders per customer, and HAVING keeps only groups with 2+ orders.

data.title: GROUP BY / HAVING cheat sheet
points: GROUP BY groups rows; each group produces one result row
SELECT columns must be in GROUP BY or wrapped in an aggregate
WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after
HAVING can use aggregate expressions; WHERE cannot
Repeat the full aggregate in HAVING — aliases are not allowed

data.text: Remember the canonical evaluation order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY. Each step refines the data, which is why you cannot reference SELECT aliases in WHERE or HAVING — those clauses run before the aliases exist.
